34461: The well-preserved theatre has a seat inscription often read as reserving places for Jews and God-fearers. The Market Gate of Miletus is reconstructed in Berlin.
34463: Capital of the empire. A church existed here before Paul arrived, as his letter to the Romans shows; Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome preaching openly. Early tradition holds that Peter and Paul were martyred here under Nero.
34464: The catacombs (from the 2nd century) contain early Christian art and inscriptions. Excavations beneath St Peter's found a 2nd-century monument (the "trophy of Gaius") at a site venerated as Peter's grave.
34466: The island where Paul's ship was wrecked on the way to Rome. Paul survived a viper's bite and healed the father of Publius, the island's chief man, and the party wintered there three months. Malta is the usual identification; Cephalonia and Mljet have been suggested as alternatives.
34467: St Paul's Bay is the traditional landing; Roman anchors recovered nearby have been linked to the wreck in popular accounts but not demonstrated.
34469: The large island south of the Aegean, probably the biblical Caphtor from which the Philistines came. Paul's ship sheltered on its south coast before the storm, and Paul left Titus there to appoint elders.
34470: Minoan palaces such as Knossos testify to Crete's Bronze Age civilisation; Roman Gortyn was the provincial capital in Paul's time.
34472: A small Aegean island where John was exiled "on account of the word of God" and received the visions of Revelation.
34473: The Cave of the Apocalypse and the Monastery of St John the Theologian (founded 1088) are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
34474: A region of central Anatolia settled by Celtic Gauls, and also a larger Roman province that included Lycaonia and Pisidia. Whether Paul's letter to the Galatians addressed ethnic Galatians in the north (Ancyra, Pessinus) or the southern cities of his first journey is a long-running debate.
34476: A town in the Lycus valley, near Laodicea and Hierapolis, whose church was founded by Epaphras. Paul's letter to the Colossians and his letter to Philemon were sent here, with the returning slave Onesimus.
34477: The mound was largely unexcavated until Turkish excavations began in 2021; the city was damaged by an earthquake around AD 60 that also struck Laodicea.
34479: A wealthy banking, textile and medical centre of the Lycus valley. Paul mentions a letter to the Laodiceans, and Revelation rebukes the church as lukewarm, rich in its own eyes but poor and blind.
34480: Excavations since 2003 have uncovered colonnaded streets, theatres, a stadium, and an early church (c. 4th century). Water reached the city through stone pipes heavy with calcium deposits, often linked with the "lukewarm" image.
34482: A prosperous port north of Ephesus. The risen Christ tells its suffering church to be faithful unto death; its bishop Polycarp was martyred here around AD 155.
34483: The Roman agora of Smyrna, rebuilt after an earthquake in 178, has been excavated in central Izmir.
34486: The former Attalid capital, a centre of the imperial cult and of healing at the Asclepieion. Revelation calls it the place "where Satan's throne is" and names the martyr Antipas.
34487: The acropolis held a famous library, a steep theatre and the Great Altar of Zeus, now reconstructed in Berlin. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
34490: A trade city known for its guilds, including dyers; Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul met at Philippi, came from here. Revelation warns the church against a prophetess it calls Jezebel.
34491: Inscriptions mention numerous trade guilds, including dyers, bronze-smiths and leather workers.
34494: The old capital of Lydia, once ruled by Croesus. Revelation tells its church it has a name for being alive but is dead, and urges it to wake up. Obadiah's "Sepharad" may refer to Sardis.
34495: Harvard-Cornell excavations uncovered a huge synagogue (3rd to 4th century) within the bath-gymnasium complex and the temple of Artemis.
34497: A city on the road to the interior, rebuilt after the earthquake of AD 17. Revelation praises its small church for keeping Christ's word and sets before it an open door.
34498: Alexander's city on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, home of a vast Jewish community where the Septuagint was produced. Apollos came from here, and Paul sailed on Alexandrian grain ships. Later it was the see of Athanasius and home of the catechetical school of Clement and Origen.
34499: Much of the ancient city lies under the modern one or the harbour; underwater surveys have mapped parts of the royal quarter and remains of the Pharos lighthouse.
34502: The main port for Rome's grain fleet on the Bay of Naples, where Paul landed and stayed a week with believers before travelling to Rome.
34505: Biblical Cush and Greek "Ethiopia" usually meant the Nile kingdom south of Egypt in modern Sudan rather than modern Ethiopia. The official baptised by Philip served the Candace, the title of Meroe's queens; the point shown is Meroe.
34506: Meroe has royal pyramids and temples of the Kushite kingdom. Ebed-melech, who rescued Jeremiah, was also a Cushite.
34508: In Paul's day "Arabia" usually meant the Nabataean kingdom east and south of Judea, whose king Aretas controlled Damascus for a time. Paul went into Arabia after his conversion, and he places Mount Sinai in Arabia; whether that means the Sinai peninsula, the Negev or northwest Arabia is debated.
34509: Petra, the Nabataean capital, with its rock-cut tombs and temples, is the best-known remains of the kingdom.
34510: The Roman province of northern Greece with Thessalonica as capital. A vision of a Macedonian man drew Paul into Europe, and its churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea gave generously to the collection for Jerusalem despite poverty.
34511: The Roman province of southern Greece, governed from Corinth, where Gallio was proconsul when Paul was brought before him. Stephanas' household were its first converts.
34514: A port on the Gulf of Adramyttium where Paul, who had walked overland from Troas, rejoined his companions' ship.
34515: The hilltop temple of Athena (6th century BC) overlooks the ancient harbour.
34517: The chief city of the island of Lesbos, where Paul's ship called on the way from Assos to Miletus.
34519: The island port where Paul's ship called on his voyage to Jerusalem. Its great bronze Colossus had fallen in an earthquake around 226 BC.
34521: A port of Lycia where Paul changed to a ship bound for Phoenicia on his way to Jerusalem.
34522: Excavations uncovered a Roman lighthouse and the Stadiasmus Patarensis, a monument listing the road distances of Roman Lycia.
34525: A small anchorage on the south coast of Crete near Lasea where Paul's ship sheltered. Against Paul's warning, the crew sailed on toward Phoenix to winter and were caught by the northeaster.
34527: The leading city of Sicily, where Paul's ship stayed three days after leaving Malta.
34528: Syracuse has a Greek theatre, a temple of Athena built into the cathedral, and extensive early Christian catacombs.
34531: A port on the toe of Italy across the Strait of Messina, where Paul's ship waited a day for a south wind before sailing to Puteoli.
34533: A stopping place on the Appian Way about 50 km from Rome where believers from Rome came out to meet Paul, and he thanked God and took courage.
34535: A city in Bithynia where Constantine convened the first ecumenical council in 325, which affirmed that the Son is of one substance with the Father against Arius. The second Council of Nicaea (787) ruled on icons. It is not mentioned in the Bible; the refs are texts central to the Nicene debate.
34536: In 2014 the remains of a submerged basilica (4th century or later) were found in Lake Iznik, possibly connected with the martyr Neophytos. The Hagia Sophia church in the town hosted the 787 council.
34540: The Greek city of Byzantium refounded by Constantine in 330 as the empire's new capital. It hosted the councils of 381, 553 and 680-681 and was the heart of Eastern Christianity until it fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
34541: Justinian's Hagia Sophia (537), the Theodosian land walls, the Hippodrome and the Basilica Cistern survive.
34543: A port in Roman North Africa where Augustine served as bishop from about 395 until his death in 430, as the Vandals besieged the city. Most of his sermons and letters were written here.
34544: The excavated Roman city includes a forum, baths, villas with mosaics and a large Christian basilica often linked with Augustine.
34546: The capital of Roman Gaul at the meeting of the Rhone and Saone. A persecution in 177 killed many Christians there, including Blandina, and Irenaeus became its bishop and wrote *Against Heresies* against the Gnostics.
34547: Roman theatres and the Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls, the traditional scene of the 177 martyrdoms, survive on the slopes of Fourviere.
34548: The great city of Roman Africa, home of Tertullian and the bishop-martyr Cyprian, and the place where Perpetua and Felicity were martyred around 203. Councils at Carthage, including those of 397 and 419, ratified the New Testament canon for the African church.
34549: Remains include the Antonine Baths, Punic ports, an amphitheatre and several large basilicas.
34551: A Saxon university town where Martin Luther taught and issued his Ninety-five Theses in 1517, the usual starting date of the Reformation. Luther's reading of Romans 1:17 on the righteousness of God was central to his theology.
34552: Luther's house, the Castle Church (where Luther and Melanchthon are buried) and the Town Church are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
34553: A city on Lake Geneva that adopted the Reformation in 1536 and where John Calvin ministered (1536-1538 and 1541-1564). His Academy (1559) trained pastors for France, Scotland and beyond, and English exiles produced the Geneva Bible (1560) here.
34556: A Hivite city whose people tricked Joshua into a treaty, leading to the battle where the sun stood still. The men of David and Ish-bosheth fought at its pool, and Solomon received his dream of wisdom at its high place.
34557: James Pritchard (1956-1962) found jar handles stamped with the name "Gibeon", confirming the site, and a great rock-cut pool with a spiral staircase, plausibly the "pool of Gibeon".
34560: A town of Judah in the Sorek valley on the Philistine border, where the cows pulling the returned ark arrived and men were struck for looking into it. Jehoash of Israel defeated Amaziah of Judah here.
34561: Excavations show an Iron Age town with a large underground water reservoir and a strong Judahite presence facing Philistia.
34565: A Gibeonite town on the border of Judah and Benjamin where the ark rested for twenty years in the house of Abinadab until David brought it to Jerusalem.
34566: Excavations from 2017 found a large Iron Age podium on the hilltop, which the excavators date to the 8th century BC and link to Israelite royal activity.
34568: Gideon's hometown in Manasseh, where the angel appeared to him under the oak and where he later set up an ephod that became a snare. The site is uncertain; Afula in the Jezreel valley (shown) and et-Taiyibeh are among the proposals.
34570: A town in Gilead near the Jabbok, named by Jacob when angels met him. Ish-bosheth reigned from it, and David took refuge there during Absalom's revolt. Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbiyeh (shown) is the leading proposal.
34572: A city of refuge in Gilead and a frontier fortress fought over by Israel and Aram. Ahab died attempting to retake it despite Micaiah's warning, and Jehu was anointed king in its camp. Tell er-Rumeith (shown) is the usual identification.
34574: A priestly town within sight of Jerusalem where Ahimelech gave David the consecrated bread and Goliath's sword; Saul had its priests massacred in revenge. It is usually placed on the ridge near Mount Scopus or el-Isawiya.
34577: A walled town of the Shephelah that David rescued from the Philistines; when God warned him its people would hand him over to Saul, he left.
34579: A major crossing of the Euphrates on today's Turkey-Syria border. Here Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Necho in 605 BC, ending Egyptian power in Syria and opening Judah to Babylon.
34580: Excavations by Woolley and T. E. Lawrence (1911-1914) and later Turkish-Italian work uncovered Neo-Hittite sculpture and destruction debris from 605 BC.
34584: A fortress city where the Jezreel valley meets the Jordan valley. The Philistines hung the bodies of Saul and his sons on its wall. In Roman times, as Scythopolis, it was the leading city of the Decapolis.
34585: Tel Beth-shean held an Egyptian garrison of the New Kingdom with stelae of Seti I and Ramesses II. Below it lie extensive Roman-Byzantine streets, a theatre and baths, ruined by the earthquake of 749.
34588: A Canaanite city guarding the route from the coast to Jerusalem. Pharaoh captured it and gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife, and Solomon rebuilt it with Hazor and Megiddo.
34589: Finds include the Gezer Calendar (found 1908), one of the earliest Hebrew inscriptions, a row of standing stones, a six-chambered gate debated as Solomonic, and boundary inscriptions naming the city.
34592: A town of the eastern Negev whose king attacked Israel in the wilderness. The Iron Age fortress guarded Judah's southern frontier.
34593: The fortress had a shrine with an altar and two incense altars and standing stones, later dismantled. Over 100 ostraca include the Eliashib archive and a reference to the "house of YHWH".
34597: A city at the springs of the Yarkon where the Philistines gathered before capturing the ark and before the battle of Gilboa. Herod rebuilt it as Antipatris, where Roman soldiers brought Paul overnight on the way to Caesarea.
34598: Tel Afek has an Egyptian governor's residence (13th century BC) with cuneiform tablets and the Ottoman fortress of Binar Bashi.
34600: The mountain of blessing above Shechem, opposite Ebal. The Samaritans regard it as the place God chose and built a temple there; the Samaritan woman asked Jesus whether worship belonged on this mountain or in Jerusalem.
34601: Yitzhak Magen's excavations uncovered the Samaritan sacred precinct (from the 5th century BC), destroyed by John Hyrcanus about 110 BC, and a Byzantine church of Mary Theotokos. Samaritans still celebrate Passover on the mountain.
34603: The mountain of curses north of Shechem, where Moses commanded an altar and stones inscribed with the law, and Joshua carried this out.
34604: Adam Zertal excavated a stone structure (1980s) he interpreted as Joshua's altar; others read it as a watchtower or farmhouse. A small lead tablet from his spoil, claimed in 2022 to bear an early curse inscription, is widely disputed.
34607: The snow-capped peak (about 2,814 m) at the northern edge of Israel whose melt feeds the Jordan. Psalm 133 uses its dew as an image of unity. Many modern scholars prefer it over Tabor as the mountain of the Transfiguration.
34609: A village near the Hill of Moreh where Saul, the night before Gilboa, consulted a medium who brought up Samuel. Its exact site near modern Ein Dor is uncertain.
34612: A town of Zebulun north of Nazareth, home of the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, who prophesied the restoration of Israel's borders under Jeroboam II.
34615: The old Median capital and a summer residence of the Persian kings. Darius' officials found Cyrus' decree authorising the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple in its archive.
34617: A settlement on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea near the caves where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found from 1947. Many scholars link it with an Essene-like community that applied Isaiah 40:3 to its life in the wilderness; others see it as a fortress or villa unrelated to the scrolls.
34618: Roland de Vaux excavated ritual baths, a scriptorium-like room and a cemetery. The caves yielded about 900 manuscripts, including copies of every Old Testament book except Esther.
34622: The place east of the Jordan where John was baptising and where Jesus later withdrew. The site shown is Al-Maghtas (Wadi Kharrar) in Jordan, opposite Jericho; some scholars instead locate it in Batanea in the far north.
34623: Al-Maghtas has Roman and Byzantine churches, pools and monastic remains and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2015. The Madaba mosaic map marks a baptism site near here.
34626: A Decapolis city above the Yarmuk gorge. Manuscripts of the Gospels vary between "Gadarenes", "Gerasenes" and "Gergesenes" for the region where Jesus freed the demoniac and the pigs rushed into the lake; many favour Kursi on the eastern shore as the actual scene.
34627: Umm Qais preserves basalt theatres, a colonnaded street and a Byzantine church. Kursi has a large 5th-century monastery and church commemorating the miracle.
34630: The town east of the Jordan where Jacob built booths after meeting Esau. Its officials refused bread to Gideon's men and were punished, and Solomon's bronze was cast in the clay nearby. Tell Deir Alla is the common identification.
34631: Plaster inscriptions found at Deir Alla in 1967 (c. 800 BC) tell of a vision of "Balaam son of Beor", the same seer named in Numbers 22-24.
34633: The port of Syrian Antioch, from which Barnabas and Saul sailed to Cyprus on their first journey.
34634: Remains include the Titus tunnel, a large rock-cut channel built in the 1st century AD to divert floodwater from the harbour.
34637: The port of Pamphylia from which Paul and Barnabas sailed home to Antioch at the end of their first journey.
34638: Hadrian's Gate (AD 130) and the old harbour survive in Antalya's old town.
34641: The port of Philippi, where Paul first set foot in Europe after sailing from Troas by way of Samothrace.
34644: A city of Lycia whose port served the Egyptian grain fleet; here the centurion transferred Paul to an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy. It was later the see of Bishop Nicholas.
34645: Lycian rock-cut tombs, a Roman theatre and the church of St Nicholas survive.
34647: A market town on the Appian Way about 65 km from Rome, where believers from Rome came out to meet Paul along with others at Three Taverns.
34649: A camp on Israel's wilderness route and later Solomon's port on the Gulf of Aqaba, from which ships sailed to Ophir; Jehoshaphat's fleet was wrecked there. Tell el-Kheleifeh (shown) was long the favoured site; Jezirat Faraun island is an alternative.
34651: A broad valley in the Shephelah between Socoh and Azekah where Israel and the Philistines faced each other and David killed Goliath.
34652: Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified hilltop town above the valley excavated 2007-2013, dates to around 1000 BC and has two gates and an early Hebrew or Canaanite ostracon; its ethnic identity is debated.
34655: The ravine separating Jerusalem's temple hill from the Mount of Olives. David crossed it fleeing Absalom, reforming kings burned idols there, and Jesus crossed it with his disciples to the garden on the night of his arrest.
34656: Its slopes hold monumental tombs such as Absalom's Pillar and the Bene Hezir tomb (2nd to 1st century BC), and Iron Age tombs at Silwan including the Royal Steward inscription.
34658: Tradition (the Acts of Thomas and the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala) holds that the apostle Thomas preached in India and died near Mylapore (Chennai). The pin marks the Malabar coast, where tradition places his landing c. AD 52.
